title: Why the Sun stays low at the pole
purpose: Teach why sunlight at the lunar south pole is low, sideways and not continuous, so the player plans power for the dark shifts.

beats.label: diagram
beats.circle: From the pole, the Sun rolls around the edge of the sky

beats.label: model

beats.rim: Tall rim: sunny {sunlit_days} days in a row

captions: The Moon spins standing almost straight up, like a top.
So at the south pole, sunlight comes in from the side.
The Sun never climbs. It rolls around the edge of the sky.
Here is how high the Sun gets in {start_year} and {end_year}. Zero is the horizon.
It stays between {lo}° and {hi}°: just a peek above or below.
That is smaller than your thumb held out at arm's length!
So up high is best. A tall crater rim can stay sunny {sunlit_days} days straight.
Down in the crater it stays dark. Even on the rim, darkness can last {dark_days} days.
ends_on: Sunlight here comes and goes. In the dark shifts, the base runs on its battery alone.
